title: Rheumatoid Atlantoaxial Instability Causing Vertebral Artery Dissection and Posterior Circulation Stroke: A Case Report
content: Rheumatoid arthritis-related diseases of the cervical spine, especially atlantoaxial subluxation with pannus, may cause a mechanical force on the V3 portion of the vertebral arteries and predispose to vertebral artery injury and posterior circulatory stroke. The report gives an account of an elderly woman with long-term seronegative inflammatory arthritis and chronic cervical degeneration presenting with sudden severe vertigo and nausea later identified to have a left anterior inferior cerebellar artery infarct. A CT angiography vascular imaging revealed left V3 vertebral artery dissection with pseudoaneurysm and no anterior circulation, and an MRI showed acute PICA territory cerebellar infarct with other small anterior circulation lesions. The cervical spine images showed chronic rheumatoid atlantoaxial changes and C1 arch malformation in keeping with the convergence of structural RA pathology and systemic vascular risk to develop mechanical vertebral artery dissection. She was medically managed on short-course dual antiplatelet therapy and then aspirin, high-intensity statin therapy, and multidisciplinary rehabilitation, and a neurosurgical examination considered her cervical disease inoperable. This case underscores the importance of early posterior circulation vascular imaging even in low-NIHSS presentations of isolated vertigo to avoid missed diagnoses. It highlights the need for diagnostic vigilance in RA patients with new posterior circulation symptoms, as prompt recognition of uncommon causes like mechanical VAD can guide timely management and improve outcomes.
